Claude Skill Scaffold Generator

Type what a Claude Agent Skill does, when Claude should use it, and any scripts, references, or assets it bundles — get a starter SKILL.md with valid YAML frontmatter and a suggested folder layout, checked for the mistakes that keep a skill from ever triggering.

Template-generated, not model-verified. This tool assembles the frontmatter and body from the fields you type — it never calls an AI model and never uploads anything. A clean result means your fields passed this tool's checks, not that Claude will invoke the skill correctly at runtime.

    2. Your SKILL.md

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a SKILL.md was generated or copied. Nothing you type — no skill name, description, or file paths — is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What does this tool actually generate?

    A starter SKILL.md file -- valid YAML frontmatter (name and description) plus a body naming any scripts, references, or assets you said the skill bundles -- and a suggested folder layout to put it in. It does not write the skill's actual instructions for you; the body is a placeholder you fill in.

    Does this tool call an AI model to write the skill?

    No. The frontmatter and body are assembled from the fields you type by a fixed template, entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and no model is called.

    Does a clean result mean Claude will actually load and use the skill correctly?

    No. This tool checks the fields you supplied -- is the name a valid slug, does the description avoid first person, is a trigger condition present -- not whether Claude will invoke the skill correctly at runtime. Write real instructions in the body, then actually try the skill before relying on it.

    Why does the description field matter this much?

    Claude decides whether to load a skill from its description alone, before reading anything else in it. A description with no concrete trigger condition, or one written in the first person as if the skill were speaking, is the most common reason a skill exists but never fires.

← Claude Skill Scaffold Generator

Claude Skill Scaffold Generator vs. writing the frontmatter by hand

Copying a sibling skill's SKILL.md and editing it catches an obviously missing field. It reliably misses a first-person opening left over from the source skill's own voice, a description with no concrete trigger condition, YAML that looks right but is subtly malformed, and a folder layout that drifts from what the body actually names — which is what this free, no-upload generator gets right by construction, in one pass.

Where copying and editing stops being enough

Anyone building a new Claude Skill already does this: open a sibling skill's SKILL.md, copy its frontmatter, and edit the fields for the new skill. For an obviously missing name or description, that catches it. The problem is the other checks below are exactly the kind of mistake that survives editing someone else's file, because the starting point was written in a different voice for a different skill.

What you're trying to get rightCopying and editing a sibling's frontmatterThis generator
The name and description fields are present at all.Works. This is the one case an edited copy reliably keeps.Also guaranteed, in the same pass as everything below.
The description is written in third person, not left in the source skill's own first-person voice."I help with..." reads as ordinary while writing it; the mismatch is invisible to the author.Checked against a first-person pattern and flagged as a caution.
The description states a concrete trigger condition, not just what the skill does.A description that explains the capability already feels complete to the person who just built it.Assembled from a separate "when Claude should use it" field, so the condition is always present.
The YAML frontmatter parses correctly -- indentation, quoting, no stray colons.Edited by hand from a working example; a small slip can still produce YAML that looks right and doesn't parse.Assembled by a fixed template from the fields you type, so the shape is correct by construction.
The name and description length stay within the practical limits this tool documents.Easy to run long while explaining a more complex skill, with no length shown while writing.Checked against dated limits and flagged if either runs long.
The suggested folder layout matches every script, reference, and asset the body actually names.The SKILL.md and the folder are two artifacts kept in sync by memory; adding one file later is easy to forget mentioning.Both generated from the same list of files you typed, so they can't drift apart.
Starting the next skill from a clean, correctly-shaped file instead of last time's edited copy.Each new skill inherits whatever the previous one's frontmatter happened to get right or wrong.One fill-in, a fresh correctly-shaped file, every time.

Copying a working sibling skill is still a reasonable way to see the expected shape, and this generator is not doing anything a careful hand edit couldn't — it is producing the same frontmatter and folder layout a careful author would, just assembling it from a fixed template automatically instead of inheriting whatever the source file happened to get right.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page assembles your SKILL.md entirely in your own browser. It never sends what you type anywhere, and it never calls an AI model.

Common questions

Can't I just copy an existing skill's frontmatter and edit it?

For catching an obviously missing name or description field, yes -- that stands out on a read. What copying and editing an existing file does not reliably catch is a first-person opening left over from the source skill's own voice, a description that reads fine but carries no concrete trigger condition, YAML indentation or quoting that looks plausible but parses wrong, and a folder layout that no longer matches the scripts, references, or assets the body actually names once you've added or removed one. Those need the same fixed template and checks applied every time, not edited by hand from a starting point written for a different skill.

Why is first-person phrasing easy to miss when you write it yourself?

Because a description written while thinking through what the skill does naturally slips into the skill's own voice -- "I help with..." reads as ordinary and even friendly to the person writing it. Claude's own documentation asks for third person specifically because the description is matched against a request, not read as the skill introducing itself, and that mismatch is invisible to the author precisely because it sounds fine out loud.

Why does forgetting a trigger cue happen so easily?

Because a description that explains what a skill does -- "formats a CSV into a PDF form" -- already feels complete to the person who just built it; the missing half is when Claude should reach for it, which requires deliberately writing out the condition rather than the capability. Skipping that step produces a description that reads as informative and still fails to trigger reliably.

What about the folder layout?

A SKILL.md written by hand and a folder built separately are two artifacts kept in sync by memory. Add a reference file after the frontmatter is already written, and it is easy to update one and forget the other -- the file exists but the SKILL.md never mentions it, or the body promises a script that was never added to the folder.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes the manual habit any Claude Skill author already has -- writing or copying a SKILL.md's frontmatter by hand. It names no competing product or company. The generator itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page assembles the file from what you type in your own browser, and nothing you type is ever uploaded.
